corpus_gaps: The corpus holds the Notaries Ordinance only in a consolidated edition current to 2024. Rule (9) of section 31 was substituted by Act No. 31 of 2022 and further altered by Act No. 6 of 2024, so the printed rule (9) is NOT the text in force in October 2019. The October 2019 opening words survive in the corpus only as the words recited as being replaced in 31-2022/s16 subsection (6), which is why that amending section is recorded as a provision here.

Rule (10) of section 31 existed at the matter reference date (it was repealed by Act No. 6 of 2024, s.3(4)) but its text is nowhere in the corpus; the repealing section does not recite it. Its content could not be checked.

Section 34 (penalty for breaches of the section 31 rules) is held only in its Act No. 31 of 2022 form, so the penalty in force in October 2019 could not be stated and no penalty provision was recorded.

Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2 is likewise held only in a post-2019 form (amended in 2022 and 2024), so it was not relied on for the number of witnesses required in October 2019; rule (8) of section 31, which is unamended, was used instead.

No provision anywhere in the corpus disqualifies an attesting witness by reason of relationship to the notary. Searches for brother, relative, relation, consanguinity, affinity, kindred, spouse, credible witness and disinterest returned nothing on point. The absence of such a rule is a negative finding drawn from the corpus, not a quotable provision.

provisions.why_relevant: This amending subsection recites verbatim the opening words of rule (9) of section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance as they stood immediately before the 2022 substitution, and therefore as they stood at the matter reference date. Those words are the operative rule for this question: a notary may attest only where the executant is known to him, or is known to at least two of the attesting witnesses.

What is recorded and relied on here is the wording it quotes as the wording it replaced, which is the rule (9) text in force at the matter reference date. The replacing wording (identity by inspection of a national identity card, passport bio-page or driving licence) came into force only in 2022 and must not be applied to this matter. This is the one entry in the map where the section_id points at an instrument later than the matter date; it is recorded this way because the corpus holds no pre-2022 edition of section 31.

provisions.why_relevant: Recorded to show what rule (9) says now and to mark the difference from the text applied to this matter. The identity-document route in these words was introduced after the matter reference date and is not available to the notary in October 2019.
provisions.temporal_note: Substituted into section 31 by Act No. 31 of 2022, s.16(6), which is after the matter reference date of October 2019. Not applied; recorded only so the verifier can see the divergence between the corpus text and the text in force at the matter date.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: he shall satisfy himself, before accepting them as witnesses, that they are persons of good repute and that they are well acquainted with the executant and know his proper name, occupation, and residence, and the witnesses shall sign a declaration at the foot of the deed or instrument that they are well acquainted with the executant and know his proper name, occupation, and residence.
provisions.why_relevant: Where the notary does not know the executant and proceeds on the witnesses, this limb obliges him to satisfy himself that the attesting witnesses are of good repute and are well acquainted with the executant and know his proper name, occupation and residence, and to have the witnesses sign a declaration to that effect. It is stated of the witnesses in the plural, so one acquainted witness is not enough.
provisions.temporal_note: This limb was in force at the matter reference date. The only change made to it since is by Act No. 6 of 2024, s.3(3), which substituted the words "he shall" for the introductory words "and in the latter case, he shall". That change is verbal and does not alter the substance relied on. In October 2019 the limb read with the introductory words "and in the latter case,", which tied it to the situation where the notary relies on the witnesses rather than on his own knowledge, which is this matter.
provisions.verifier_note: Excerpt confirmed verbatim against the consolidated (post-2024) text, and the substance was in force in October 2019, but the quoted words are not the 2019 wording exactly: until Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(3) the limb opened "and in the latter case, he shall satisfy himself", which the map's temporal_note states correctly.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument to which he is a party.
provisions.why_relevant: This is the only personal disqualification the rules impose on the notary himself. It bars him where he is a party to the deed. It does not reach a case where a relative of his signs as an attesting witness, and no other rule in section 31 disqualifies a witness by reason of kinship to the notary. The rule is therefore what supports the conclusion that the fraternal relationship is not, of itself, a bar to attestation.
provisions.temporal_note: In force since 1907 and untouched by Acts No. 20 of 1976, No. 47 of 2011, No. 13 of 2013, No. 31 of 2022 or No. 6 of 2024 on the amendment record held in the corpus. In force at the matter reference date.

provisions.why_relevant: Fixes the minimum of two attesting witnesses, which is what makes the plural in the acquaintance and declaration limb bite: there must be at least two attesting witnesses, and the acquaintance requirement is stated of them collectively.
provisions.temporal_note: Untouched by any amending Act recorded against section 31 in the corpus. In force at the matter reference date.

questions.authority_requirement_reason: The question is whether the statutory rules of practice permit attestation on these facts. Rule (9) of section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance states the identification condition exhaustively, rule (8) fixes the number of attesting witnesses, and rule (13) states the only personal bar on the notary. Nothing in the answer depends on judicial authority or on Roman-Dutch common law. The point about the witness being the notary's brother is answered by the absence of any disqualifying rule in the Ordinance, which is a reading of the statute rather than a proposition of case law.

legal_issues.issue: Whether a notary who does not himself know the executant may attest the deed when only one of the two attesting witnesses is well acquainted with the executant.
Whether an attesting witness who is the notary's own brother is disqualified from attesting, or bars the notary from attesting the deed.
Which text of rule (9) of section 31 governs a deed attested in October 2019, given the substitutions made in 2022 and 2024.

questions.hop_count_basis: Three necessary linked steps. First, fix the text of rule (9) in force in October 2019, which is reachable only through the wording recited as replaced in s.16(6) of Act No. 31 of 2022. Second, apply the acquaintance and declaration limb of the same rule, which qualifies the first limb and is stated of the attesting witnesses in the plural. Third, cross to rule (13), the only personal disqualification imposed on the notary, to dispose of the separate point that the acquainted witness is the notary's brother.

enrichment.original_background: The Notary does not know the executant but he is well known to one of the witnesses. This witness is the Notary's own brother.
enrichment.enriched_background: Mr. K. A. Dharmasena is a notary public authorised to practise in Sinhala in the Colombo judicial zone. On 12 October 2019 Mr. Sunil Rajapaksha comes to his office and asks him to attest a deed of transfer, drawn by the notary himself, by which Mr. Rajapaksha transfers to Ms. Nirmali Fernando an allotment of land at Maharagama; Mr. Rajapaksha produces the title deed by which he bought the land. He brings two persons with him to sign as attesting witnesses. The Notary does not know the executant but he is well known to one of the witnesses. This witness is the Notary's own brother, Mr. P. A. Dharmasena, a retired schoolmaster of good repute who has lived next door to Mr. Rajapaksha for many years and can state his full name, his occupation and his address. The second witness is a clerk from the shop next to the notary's office who had never met Mr. Rajapaksha before that morning and cannot say what his occupation or his residence is. Mr. Rajapaksha produces no identity card, passport or driving licence. The notary is not a party to the deed and has no interest in the land.

added_facts.fact: The notary is Mr. K. A. Dharmasena, practising in Sinhala in the Colombo judicial zone; the executant is Mr. Sunil Rajapaksha; the transferee is Ms. Nirmali Fernando; the instrument is a deed of transfer of an allotment of land at Maharagama, presented for attestation on 12 October 2019, and the executant produces the title deed under which he bought the land.
added_facts.reason: The original scenario names no party, no instrument and no document, which are the three missing fact types recorded for this question. Naming them makes the scenario determinate without changing the legal question.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Without an identified deed and identified parties the attestation rules cannot be applied to a concrete instrument; the answer would be a statement of the rules in the abstract.

added_facts.fact: The witness who is the notary's brother, Mr. P. A. Dharmasena, is a retired schoolmaster of good repute, has lived next door to the executant for many years, and can state the executant's proper name, occupation and residence.
added_facts.reason: Makes the phrase well known to one of the witnesses precise in the terms the rule uses, so that this witness plainly satisfies the acquaintance requirement and the analysis turns on the second witness rather than on an ambiguity about the first.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If this witness were not of good repute or could not state the executant's name, occupation and residence, the deed would fail the acquaintance requirement on both witnesses rather than on one, and the reasoning would be shorter.

added_facts.fact: The second attesting witness is a clerk from the shop next to the notary's office who had never met the executant before that morning and cannot say what the executant's occupation or residence is.
added_facts.reason: The original scenario says the executant is well known to one of the witnesses and is silent about the other. The rule turns on whether the executant is known to at least two attesting witnesses, so the standing of the second witness has to be settled for the question to have a determinate answer.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the second witness were also well acquainted with the executant and could state his name, occupation and residence, the identification requirement would be satisfied and the notary could attest.

added_facts.fact: The executant produces no national identity card, passport or driving licence to the notary.
added_facts.reason: Closes an alternative route that exists only under the text of rule (9) substituted in 2022. At the matter reference date of October 2019 identification by inspecting an identity document was not an available route, so the fact does not change the answer for this matter; it is added so that a reader working from the current consolidated text cannot mistake the scenario.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Under the rule as it stands after 2022 the production of an identity card would satisfy the identification limb; at the matter reference date it would make no difference.

added_facts.fact: The notary is not a party to the deed and has no interest in the land transferred.
added_facts.reason: The only personal bar the rules place on the notary is that he must not attest a deed to which he is a party. Stating that he is not a party keeps the brother point on its own footing instead of leaving that bar open.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the notary were a party to the deed he would be barred from attesting outright, and the identification point would not need to be reached.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether the notary may attest this deed of transfer when he does not himself know the executant, when only one of the two attesting witnesses is well acquainted with the executant, and when that witness is the notary's own brother.
gold_answer_draft.rule: At October 2019 rule (9) of section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance provided that a notary shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing the same be known to him or to at least two of the attesting witnesses thereto; those words are recited as the words replaced by section 16(6) of the Notaries (Amendment) Act, No. 31 of 2022, and the replacing words, which allow identification by inspection of a national identity card, passport bio-page or driving licence, took effect only in 2022 and do not govern this deed. Where the notary relies on the witnesses rather than on his own knowledge, the same rule (9) requires him to satisfy himself, before accepting them as witnesses, that they are persons of good repute and that they are well acquainted with the executant and know his proper name, occupation and residence, and requires the witnesses to sign a declaration at the foot of the deed to that effect; the requirement is stated of the witnesses in the plural, and rule (8) of section 31 requires at least two witnesses to subscribe their signatures in letters. Section 31 imposes only one personal bar on the notary himself: by rule (13) he shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument to which he is a party. No rule in section 31 disqualifies an attesting witness by reason of his relationship to the notary.
gold_answer_draft.application: The notary does not know Mr. Rajapaksha, so he can proceed only on the witness limb of rule (9), which needs the executant to be known to at least two of the attesting witnesses. Only the brother, Mr. P. A. Dharmasena, is well acquainted with Mr. Rajapaksha and able to state his proper name, occupation and residence; the second witness had never met him before that morning and cannot state his occupation or residence. The executant is therefore known to one attesting witness only, the notary cannot satisfy himself of the matters rule (9) requires as to both witnesses, and both witnesses cannot honestly sign the declaration at the foot of the deed. The identity-document route was not open in October 2019 and in any event no such document was produced. The brother relationship is a separate point and does not add a bar: rule (13) prevents the notary attesting only where he is a party, and he is not a party to or interested in this deed, while nothing in section 31 excludes a relative of the notary from signing as an attesting witness. The weight later given to his evidence is another matter, but the rules do not disqualify him.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The notary could not properly attest this deed as the facts stand, and the reason is the identification requirement rather than the family connection. The executant was neither known to the notary nor known to at least two of the attesting witnesses. The brother is not disqualified by being the notary's brother, so the defect is cured if a second witness who is of good repute and well acquainted with the executant, and able to state his proper name, occupation and residence, is brought in and both witnesses sign the required declaration at the foot of the deed; the notary may then attest.

answer_claims.claim_text: At the matter reference date a notary was forbidden to authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing it was known to him or to at least two of the attesting witnesses.

Identification of an executant by inspection of a national identity card, passport bio-page or driving licence was introduced into rule (9) only in 2022 and was not an available route in October 2019.

Where the notary relies on the attesting witnesses instead of his own knowledge, he must satisfy himself before accepting them that they are persons of good repute and are well acquainted with the executant and know his proper name, occupation and residence, and the witnesses must sign a declaration at the foot of the deed to that effect.
At least two witnesses must subscribe their signatures in letters to the deed, so the acquaintance and declaration requirement applies to two or more attesting witnesses and not to one.

The only personal bar section 31 places on the notary is that he shall not authenticate or attest a deed or instrument to which he is a party, and no rule in section 31 disqualifies an attesting witness because he is related to the notary.
Because the notary does not know the executant, he can attest only on the footing that the executant is known to at least two of the attesting witnesses.

Only one of the two attesting witnesses, the notary's brother, is well acquainted with the executant and able to state his proper name, occupation and residence; the second witness had never met the executant and cannot state his occupation or residence.

The executant is therefore not known to at least two of the attesting witnesses, and the two witnesses cannot both sign the declaration that they are well acquainted with him and know his proper name, occupation and residence.
No identity document was produced, so even on the text that came into force after the matter reference date the identification limb would not be satisfied by inspection.

The notary is not a party to this deed and has no interest in the land, so the single personal bar in rule (13) is not engaged, and the brother is not disqualified from acting as an attesting witness by his relationship to the notary.
On these facts the notary could not properly attest the deed, because the executant was neither known to him nor known to at least two of the attesting witnesses.

The bar arises from the identification requirement and not from the fact that the acquainted witness is the notary's brother, so the notary may attest once a second witness of good repute who is well acquainted with the executant is brought in and both witnesses sign the required declaration.
